summary:
I've been putting most of my Claude time into Keikochō, a Japanese-learning app I build for myself. The engine treats grammar as data — 32 lexemes, 222 frames, thousands of generated sentences — rather than hand-written lesson content, so adding a new verb form means writing a rule, not authoring hundreds of example sentences by hand.

The harder lessons came from testing. I've been keeping a running log of guards that pass while checking nothing: a test that read the old location of moved data, a dedupe keyed on the wrong field so 43% of one quiz type couldn't be answered wrong, a negative assertion that could never have failed because the fixture guaranteed it. None of these threw errors — they just quietly stopped measuring what they were supposed to. The fix is usually the same shape: build the test on a fixture you construct yourself, not on content that happens to exercise it today, because finishing the content is exactly when the test goes blind.

I also shipped a two-page rehearsal tool for a work farewell — English and Japanese audio, timed for a recorded voice note. The first version worked fine as a preview artifact and then didn't load at all as a real page, because an artifact build is a fragment (no viewport meta, so mobile Safari renders it zoomed out) and its audio was base64-encoded into one document instead of served as files. Splitting it into real static assets fixed both.

On the infrastructure side, most of what I touch is automation plumbing for a personal AI assistant I run at home — model routing, tool wiring, that kind of thing. One worth mentioning: I set up an A/B test between two local models on tool-calling reliability, expecting a clear winner going in. Both scored identically on the benchmark, which turned out to be the actual finding — the benchmark was too easy to tell them apart, not that the models were equivalent. Sometimes the useful result is realizing your test doesn't discriminate.

highlights.oneLiner: Automation plumbing for a personal AI assistant — model routing, tool wiring.
A/B tested two local models on tool-calling; benchmark couldn't tell them apart.
